<![CDATA[ <p>The first thing I was told when I embarked on learning web standards about twelve years ago was, "don't use tables for layout." This was sound advice in spirit, but not very well qualified. As a result, there have been some unfortunate interpretations. Using table markup inevitably results in a visual layout, which has led some to abandon HTML tables altogether. Tables: <em>bad</em>.</p> <p>The lesson in "don't use tables for layout" is not to use HTML elements in ways for which they were not intended. Twelve years ago, the idea that I would be coding HTML 'wrong' was enough to put me off making such classic blunders. Vanity is not a real reason, though.</p> <p>The real reason — the reason it's a bad practice — is how it affects the user. Table markup, starting at <code><table></code> and including <code><th></code>, <code><td></code> <em>et al</em>, tells browsers to pass on certain information and produce certain behaviors. Someone using assistive software such as a screen reader will become subject to this information and behavior. </p> <p>When table markup contains non-tabular content, it messes with blind users' expectations. It's not a page layout to them; it's a data table that doesn't make sense. If they're sighted or partially sighted and running a screen reader it's <em>both</em>, which is arguably even more confusing.</p> <p>Our way of judging web technologies is oddly epochal. We believe that one epoch — the epoch of CSS Flexbox, for example — should end as it ushers in the new epoch of CSS Grid. But like <code><div></code>-based page layouts and data tables, these are actually complementary things that can co-exist. You just need to know where to use one, and where the other.</p> <p>In this article, I'll be exploring how to create inclusive data tables: ones that are screen reader accessible, responsive, and as ergonomic as possible for everyone. First, though, I want to show you a trick for fixing an old layout table.</p> <hr> <h2 id="thepresentationrole">The presentation role</h2> <p>WAI-ARIA can be a helpful tool because it allows you to add and extend semantic information in HTML. For example, adding <code>aria-pressed</code> to a standard button makes it a toggle button to browsers and, therefore, assistive software. But did you know you can also use WAI-ARIA to take semantics away? That is, the following two elements are each semantically indeterminate to a screen reader. Neither are a 'button'.</p> <pre><code><button role="presentation">Press me</button> <span>Press me</span> </code></pre> <p>Most of the time you'll only want to add semantics where they are useful, rather than choosing elements for their appearance and removing the semantics where they aren't needed. But sometimes reverse engineering accessibility information is the most efficient way to make good of a bad decision like a layout table.</p> <p>Applying <code>role="presentation"</code> to a <code><table></code> element removes all of that table's semantics, and therefore elicited behaviors, in screen readers. It is as if it was constructed using semantically unassuming <code><div></code>s all along.</p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/03/table_presentation.svg" alt="On the left a table element contains <td> elements. On the right a table element with role = presentation has div elements"></p> <p>Note that <code>role="presentation"</code> and <code>role="none"</code> are synonymous. The first is more longstanding and better supported.</p> <p>In 2018, there are much better layout solutions than <code><table></code>s anyway, so there's no advantage in using them for any new layout you're trying out.</p> <h2 id="truedatatables">True data tables</h2> <p>A typical layout table consists of a <code><table></code> container, some <code><tr></code>s, and some <code><td></code>s inside them.</p> <pre><code><table> <tr> <td><img src="some/image" alt=""></td> <td>Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><img src="some/other/image" alt=""></td> <td>Integer vitae blandit nisi.</td> </tr> </table> </code></pre> <p>The semantics issue to one side, these are all the elements you really need to achieve a visual layout. You have your rows and columns, like a grid. </p> <p>Unfortunately, even where our <em>intention</em> is to manufacture a data table, we still tend to think visually only: "If it looks like a table, I'm good." But the following does not make an accessible table.</p> <pre><code><table> <tr> <td>Column header 1</td> <td>Column header 2</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Row one, first cell</td> <td>Row one, second cell</td> </tr> </table> </code></pre> <p>Why? Because our column headers — semantically speaking — are just bog standard table elements. There's nothing here to explicitly say they are headers except the text (which is likely to be less clear in a real example than "Column header 1"). Instead, we need to make them <code><th></code> elements.</p> <pre><code><table> <tr> <th>Column header 1</th> <th>Column header 2</th> </tr> <tr> <td>Row one, first cell</td> <td>Row one, second cell</td> </tr> </table> </code></pre> <p>Using column headers in this way is not just to be 'semantically correct'. There is a manifest effect on screen reader behavior. Now, if I use my screen reader to navigate to a row cell, it will read out the header under which it sits, letting me know which column I am currently in.</p> <h3 id="rowheaders">Row headers</h3> <p>It's possible to have both column and row headers in data tables. I can't think of any kind of data for which row headers are strictly <em>necessary</em> for comprehension, but sometimes it feels like the <em>key</em> value for a table row should be on the left, and highlighted as such.</p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/03/row_headers.png" alt="table with row headers down left hand side"></p> <p>The trouble is, unless you state it explicitly, it isn't clear whether a header labels cells below it or to its right. That's where the <code>scope</code> attribute comes in. For column headers you use <code>scope="col"</code> and for row headers you use <code>scope="row"</code>.</p> <p>Here's an example for fuel prices that I was working on for <a href="https://bulb.co.uk/">Bulb</a> recently. </p> <pre><code><table> <tbody> <tr> <th scope="col">Region</th> <th scope="col">Electricity</th> <th scope="col">Gas</th> </tr> <tr> <th scope="row">East England</th> <td>10.40</td> <td>2.31</td> </tr> <tr> <th scope="row">East Midlands</th> <td>10.55</td> <td>2.77</td> </tr> <tr> <th scope="row">London</th> <td>10.10</td> <td>2.48</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> </code></pre> <p>Note that not setting row headers does not make a nonsense of the data; it just adds extra clarity and context. For a table that uses both column and row headers, some screen readers will announce both the column and row labels for each of the data cells.</p> <div role="complementary"> <h3>Using tables with screen readers</h3> <p>Complex interfaces and widgets tend to have special behaviors and associated keyboard shortcuts in screen readers, and tables are no different.</p> <p>JAWS, NVDA, and VoiceOver each provide the <kbd>T</kbd> key to move between tables on the page. To navigate between table cells, you use your arrow keys. When arriving at a table, you are typically informed of how many columns and rows it contains. The <code><caption></code>, if present, is also read out.</p> <p>When you switch between cells across columns, the new column header is announced, along with the numeric placement of the column (e.g. "column 3 of 4"), and the content of the cell itself. When you switch between cells across rows, the new row header is announced, along with the numeric placement of the row (e.g. "row 5 of 8"), and the content of the cell itself.</p> <style>.embed-container { position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden; max-width: 100%; } .embed-container iframe, .embed-container object, .embed-container embed { position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; }</style><div class="embed-container"><iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/tlpQ0d2ADNo" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></div> </div> <h2 id="captions">Captions</h2> <p>There used to be two ways to provide descriptive information directly to tables: <code><caption></code> and <code><summary></code>. The <code><summary></code> element was deprecated in HTML5, so should be avoided. The <code><caption></code> element is superior regardless, because it provides a visual and screen reader accessible label. The <code><summary></code> element works more like an <code>alt</code> attribute and is not visible. Since the table itself provides textual information, such a summary should not be necessary.</p> <p>Not all tables necessarily need captions, but it's recommended you either provide a caption or precede the table with a heading. That is, unless the table is inside a <code><figure></code> with a <code><figcaption></code>. As the name suggestions, the <code><figcaption></code> is a kind of caption on its own, and will suffice.</p> <p>The advantage of a caption over a heading is that it is read out when a screen reader user encounters the table directly, using the <kbd>T</kbd> shortcut key. Fortunately <a href="http://juicystudio.com/article/HTML5_caption_element_headings.php">HTML5 lets you place headings <em>inside</em> captions</a>, which is the best of both worlds and highly recommended where you know what level the heading should be ahead of time.</p> <figure> <img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/03/table_keys.png" alt="Shows the three different shortcut keys, t, h, and the down arrow key, pointing down towards the table"> <figcaption>By using a heading inside the table <code><caption></code>, there are now three ways to discover the table: by table shortcut, heading shortcut, or just by browsing downwards.</figcaption> </figure> <h2 id="adatadriventablecomponent">A data-driven table component</h2> <p>That pretty much covers basic tables and how to make them accessible. The trouble is, they're such a pain to code by hand, and most WYSIWYG tools for creating tables do not output decent markup, with the necessary headers in the correct places.</p> <p>Instead, let's create a component that accepts data and outputs an accessible table automatically. In React, we can supply the headers and rows as props. In the headers' case we just need an array. For the rows: an array of arrays (or "two-dimensional" array).</p> <pre><code>const headers = ['Band', 'Singer', 'Inception', 'Label']; const rows = [ ['Napalm Death', 'Barney Greenway', '1981', 'Century Media'], ['Carcass', 'Jeff Walker', '1985', 'Earache'], ['Extreme Noise Terror', 'Dean Jones', '1985', 'Candlelight'], ['Discordance Axis', 'Jon Chang', '1992', 'Hydrahead'] ]; </code></pre> <p>Now the <code>Table</code> component just needs those <code>const</code>s passed in.</p> <pre><code><Table rows={rows} headers={headers} /> </code></pre> <p>One of the best and worst things about HTML is that it's forgiving. You can write badly formed, inaccessible HTML and the browser will still render it without error. This makes the web platform inclusive of beginners, and those creating rule-breaking experiments. But it doesn't hold us to account when we're trying to create well-formed code that's compatible with all parsers, including assistive technologies.</p> <p>By deferring the well-formed part to arrays, which expect a very specific structure, we can catch errors there. Where the arrays are well-formed, we can generate accessible markup from them, automatically.</p> <p>Here's how the basic component that handles this might look:</p> <pre><code>class Table extends React.Component { render() { return ( <table> <tr> {this.props.headers.map((header, i) => <th scope="col" key={i}>{header}</th> )} </tr> {this.props.rows.map((row, i) => <tr key={i}> {row.map((cell, i) => <td key={i}>{cell}</td> )} </tr> )} </table> ); } } </code></pre> <p>If you don't supply arrays for the <code>headers</code> and <code>rows</code> props things are going to go spectacularly wrong, so if you dig <em>'not a function'</em> errors, look forward. </p> <p>Perhaps, though, it would be better to catch those errors early and output a more helpful message. That's where 'prop types' can be useful.</p> <pre><code>Table.propTypes = { headers: PropTypes.array.required, rows: PropTypes.array.required }; </code></pre> <p>Of course, if you're using Typescript, you'll probably be handing this with an <a href="https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/interfaces.html">interface</a> instead. I personally find the extreme rigidity and perplexing syntax of Typescript in React <em>a bit much</em>. I'm told it's great for when you're writing complex enterprise software, but if you mostly deal with with small projects and codebases, life is probably too short.</p> <h3 id="supportingrowheaders">Supporting row headers</h3> <p>Supporting the option of row headers is a cinch. We just need to know if the author has included a <code>rowHeaders</code> prop. Then we can transform the first cell of each row into a <code><th></code> with <code>scope="row"</code>.</p> <pre><code><tr key={i}> {row.map((cell, i) => (this.props.rowHeaders && i < 1) ? ( <th scope="row" key={i}>{cell}</th> ) : ( <td key={i}>{cell}</td> ) )} </tr> </code></pre> <p>In my table about grindcore bands, this makes a lot of sense since the bands named down the left hand side are the basis for all the other information.</p> <p>Here's a <a href="https://codepen.io/heydon/pen/GxvXpX">codePen demo of the basic table component</a>, coming in at just 25 lines:</p> <div> <p data-height="265" data-theme-id="0" data-slug-hash="zJdxwQ" data-default-tab="js,result" data-user="heydon" data-embed-version="2" data-pen-title="React Inclusive Table Component " class="codepen">See the Pen <a href="https://codepen.io/heydon/pen/zJdxwQ">React Inclusive Table Component </a> by Heydon (<a href="https://codepen.io/heydon">@heydon</a>) on <a href="https://codepen.io">CodePen</a>.</p> <script async src="https://static.codepen.io/assets/embed/ei.js"></script> </div> <h2 id="goingresponsive">Going responsive</h2> <p>Responsive tables are one of those areas where the accessible solution is more about what you don't do than what you do. As <a href="http://adrianroselli.com/2018/02/tables-css-display-properties-and-aria.html#TheTweet">Adrian Roselli recently noted</a>, using CSS display properties to change table layout has a tendency to remove the underlying table semantics. This probably shouldn't happen, because it messes with the <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/html-design-principles/#separation-of-concerns">separation of concerns principle</a>. <strong>It happens anyway</strong>.</p> <p>This isn't the only reason it's a bad idea to change the way tables are displayed. Visually speaking, it's not really the same table — or much of a table at all — if the columns and rows collapse on top of one another. Instead, we want to provide access to the same visual and semantic structure regardless of the space available. </p> <p>It's as simple as letting the table's parent element scroll horizontally.</p> <pre><code>.table-container { overflow-x: auto; } </code></pre> <h3 id="keyboardsupport">Keyboard support</h3> <p>Okay, it's not <em>quite</em> that simple. As you may recall from <a href="https://inclusive-components.design/a-content-slider/">A Content Slider</a>, we need to make the scrollable element focusable so it can be operated by keyboard. That's just a case of adding <code>tabindex="0"</code>. But since screen reader users will be able to focus it too, we need to provide some context for them.</p> <p>In this case, I'll use the table's <code><caption></code> to label the scrollable region using <code>aria-labelledby</code>.</p> <pre><code><div class="table-container" tabindex="0" role="group" aria-labelledby="caption"> <table> <caption id="caption">Grindcore bands</caption> <!-- table content --> </table> </div> </code></pre> <h4 id="notes">Notes</h4> <ol> <li>As I wrote in <a href="http://www.heydonworks.com/article/aria-label-is-a-xenophobe">ARIA-label Is A Xenophobe</a>, translation services like Google's don't translate the <code>aria-label</code> attribute, so it's better to label using an element's text node. We can do this with <code>aria-labelledby</code>. The unique cipher shared by <code>aria-labelledby</code> and the <code>id</code> can be generated in React using <code>Math.random()</code>. </li> <li>You can't use <code>aria-labelledby</code> just anywhere. The element has to have an appropriate <code>role</code>. Here I'm using the fairly generic <code>group</code> role for this purpose. From <a href="https://www.w3.org/WAI/PF/aria/roles#group">the spec' on <code>group</code></a>: <em>"A set of user interface objects which are not intended to be included in a page summary or table of contents by assistive technologies."</em> </li> </ol> <h3 id="onlyfocusablewherescrollable">Only focusable where scrollable</h3> <p>Of course, we don't want to make the table container focusable <em>unless</em> its contents overflow. Otherwise we're adding a tab stop to the focus order which doesn't do anything. In my opinion, that would be a fail under <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/UNDERSTANDING-WCAG20/navigation-mechanisms-focus-order.html">2.4.3 Focus Order</a>. Giving keyboard users elements to focus which don't actually do anything is confusing and obstructive.</p> <p>What we can do is detect whether the content overflows on page load (or the component mounting) by adding <code>tabindex="0"</code> only if <code>scrollWidth</code> exceeds <code>clientWidth</code> for the container. We can use a ref (<code>this.container</code>) for this purpose.</p> <pre><code>componentDidMount() { const {scrollWidth, clientWidth} = this.container; let scrollable = scrollWidth > clientWidth; this.setState({ tabindex: scrollable ? '0' : null }); } </code></pre> <p>(Thanks to Almero Steyn for the <a href="https://github.com/Heydon/react-sortable-table-demo/pull/3">note on string <code>ref</code> deprecation</a>. As he pointed out, in React 16.3 you define the <code>ref</code> in the constructor like <code>this.container = React.createRef();</code>. Then you just need to add <code>ref={this.container}</code> on the container element.)</p> <p>Here's a truncated version of the script, showing how I use state to switch the <code>tabindex</code> value via the <code>componentDidMount</code> lifecycle function.</p> <pre><code>class Table extends React.Component { constructor(props) { super(props) this.state = { tabindex: null } } componentDidMount() { let container = ReactDOM.findDOMNode(this.refs.container); let scrollable = container.scrollWidth > container.clientWidth; this.setState({ tabindex: scrollable ? '0' : null }); } render() { const captionID = 'caption-' + Math.random().toString(36).substr(2, 9); return ( <div className="table-container" ref="container" tabIndex={this.state.tabindex} aria-labelledby={captionID} > <!-- table here --> </div> ); } } </code></pre> <h3 id="perceivedaffordance">Perceived affordance</h3> <p>It's not enough that users can scroll the table. They also need to know they <em>can</em> scroll the table. Fortunately, given our table cell border style, it should be obvious when the table is cut off, indicating that some content is out of view.</p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/03/cut_off.png" alt="Table visibly cut off to the right where there is no border."></p> <p>We can do one better, just to be safe, and hook into the state to display a message in the caption:</p> <pre><code>{this.state.tabindex === '0' && <div> <small>(scroll to see more)</small> </div> } </code></pre> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/03/scrollable_with_help.png" alt="Under the caption is the text 'scroll to see more'"></p> <p>This text will also form part of the scrollable container's label (via the <code>aria-labelledby</code> association discussed earlier). In a screen reader, when the scrollable container is focused you will hear something similar to <em>"Grindcore bands, open parenthesis, scroll to see more, close parenthesis, group."</em> In other words, this extra message adds clarification non-visually too.</p> <h3 id="verynarrowviewports">Very narrow viewports</h3> <p>The preceding works for wide tables (with many columns) or narrow viewports. <em>Very</em> narrow viewports might want something a bit more radical, though. If you can barely see one column at a time, the viewing experience is pretty terrible — even if you <em>can</em> physically scroll the other columns into view by touch.</p> <p>Instead, for very narrow (one column) viewports, we can present the data using a different structure, with headings and definition lists.</p> <ul> <li><code><caption></code> → <code><h2></code></li> <li><code><th scope="row"></code> → <code><h3></code></li> <li><code><th scope="col"></code> → <code><dt></code></li> <li><code><td></code> → <code><dd></code></li> </ul> <p>This structure is much more suited to mobile, where users are more accustomed to scrolling vertically. It's also accessible, just in a different way.</p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/03/mobile.png" alt="Phone layout. One column featuring definition titles side by side with their definitions"></p> <p>Here's what the JSX might look like:</p> <pre><code><div className="lists-container"> <h2>{this.props.caption}</h2> {this.props.rows.map((row, i) => <div key={i}> <h3>{row[0]}</h3> <dl> {this.props.headers.map((header, i) => i > 0 && <React.Fragment key={i}> <dt>{header}</dt> <dd>{row[i]}</dd> </React.Fragment> )} </dl> </div> )} </div> </code></pre> <p>Note the use of <code>Fragment</code>. This allows us to output the unwrapped sibling <code><dt></code> and <code><dd></code> elements for our <code><dl></code> structure. A <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1937#issuecomment-256119695">recent change to the spec'</a> has made it permissible to wrap <code><dt></code>/<code><dd></code> pairs in <code><div></code>s (thanks to <a href="https://twitter.com/g16n">Gunnar</a> for contacting me about this). But we can't be sure it won't cause parsing issues for now, and we don't need the wrappers here anyway.</p> <p>All that's left to do is show/hide the equivalent interfaces at the appropriate viewport widths. For example:</p> <pre><code>@media (min-width: 400px) { .table-container { display: block; } .lists-container { display: none; } } </code></pre> <p>For extremely large data sets, having both interfaces in the DOM will bloat an already large DOM tree. However, in most cases this is the more performant solution compared with dynamically reconstituting the DOM via <code>matchMedia</code> or (worse still) listening to the <code>resize</code> event. </p> <p>If you're loading dynamic data, you don't have to worry about the two interfaces staying in sync: they are based directly on the same source.</p> <h2 id="sortabletables">Sortable tables</h2> <p>Let's give users some <a href="http://inclusivedesignprinciples.org/#give-control">control</a> over how the content is sorted. After all, we already have the data in a sortable format — a two-dimensional array. </p> <p>Of course, with such a small data set, just for demonstration purposes, sorting is not really needed. But let's implement it anyway, for cases where it does make things easier. The great thing about React props, is we can easily turn the functionality on or off.</p> <p>Inside each column header we can provide a sorting button:</p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/03/sort_buttons.png" alt="Each column header has a sorting button next to it featuring an arrow pointing both up and down"></p> <p>These can toggle between sorting the data by the column in either an ascending or descending order. Communicating the sorting method is the job of the <code>aria-sort</code> property. Note that it works most reliably in conjunction with an explicit <code>role="columnheader"</code>.</p> <p>Here's the inception column, communicating an ascending sort (lowest value top) to screen readers. The other possible values are <code>descending</code> and <code>none</code>.</p> <pre><code><th scope="col" role="columnheader" aria-sort="ascending"> Inception <button>sort</button> </th> </code></pre> <p>Not all screen readers support <code>aria-sort</code>, but a sorting button label of <em>"sort by [column label]"</em> makes things clear enough to those who do not have the sorting state reported. You could go one better by adapting the label to <em>"sort by [column label] in ['ascending'|'descending'] order"</em>. </p> <pre><code>aria-label={`sort by ${header} in ${this.state.sortDir !== 'ascending' ? 'ascending' : 'descending'} order`} </code></pre> <h3 id="iconography">Iconography</h3> <p>Visually, the sort order should be fairly clear by glancing down the column in hand, but we can go one better by providing icons that communicate one of three states:</p> <ul> <li>↕ = it's sortable, but not sorted</li> <li>↑ = It's sorted by this column, in ascending order</li> <li>↓ = It's sorted by this column, is descending order</li> </ul> <p>As ever, it's advantageous to use an SVG. </p> <ul> <li>SVGs scale without degredation, making zoom more pleasant</li> <li>SVGs using <code>currentColor</code> respect Windows High Contrast settings</li> <li>SVGs can be constructed efficiently from shape and line elements</li> <li>SVGs are markup and their different parts can be targeted individually</li> </ul> <p>That last advantage is not something I've explored on <a href="https://inclusive-components.design">inclusive-components.design</a> before, but is ideal here because each arrow is made of two or more lines. Consider the following <code>Arrow</code> component.</p> <pre><code>const Arrow = props => { let ascending = props.sortDir === 'ascending'; return ( <svg viewBox="0 0 100 200" width="100" height="200"> {!(!ascending && props.isCurrent) && <polyline points="20 50, 50 20, 80 50"></polyline> } <line x1="50" y1="20" x2="50" y2="180"></line> {!(ascending && props.isCurrent) && <polyline points="20 150, 50 180, 80 150"></polyline> } </svg> ); } </code></pre> <p>Logic is passed in from the parent component via props (<code>sortDir</code> and <code>current</code>) to conditionally show the different <code>polyline</code> arrow heads. For example, the final <code>polyline</code> is only shown if the following are true.</p> <ul> <li>The sort order isn't ascending</li> <li>This isn't the current sorting column</li> </ul> <p><strong>Warning:</strong> Technically here I am using the arrow to express the button's current state, not the state pressing it will achieve. In many circumstances (and as discussed in <a href="https://inclusive-components.design/toggle-button/">Toggle Buttons</a>) this is a mistake. The important thing here is the <em>change</em> in arrow direction as one toggles, communicating the switch in polarity.</p> <div role="complementary"> <h4>A note on the grid role</h4> <p>WAI-ARIA provides a role, <code>grid</code>, that is closely associated with tables. This role is intended to be paired with specific keyboard behavior, letting keyboard users navigate table cells as they would be able via screen reader software (using their arrow keys).</p> <p>You do <em>not</em> need to use the <code>grid</code> role to make most tables accessible to screen readers. The <code>grid</code>-related behavior should only be implemented where users <em>not</em> running screen reader software need to easily access each cell to interact with it. One example might be a date picker where each date is clickable within a grid representation of a calendar month.</p> </div> <h3 id="performance">Performance</h3> <p>The sorting function itself should look something like this, and uses the <code>sort</code> method:</p> <pre><code> sortBy(i) { let sortDir; let ascending = this.state.sortDir === 'ascending'; if (i === this.state.sortedBy) { sortDir = !ascending ? 'ascending' : 'descending'; } else { sortDir = 'ascending'; } this.setState(prevState => ({ rows: prevState.rows.slice(0).sort((a, b) => sortDir === 'ascending' ? a[i] > b[i] : a[i] < b[i]), sortedBy: i, sortDir: sortDir })); } </code></pre> <p>Note the use of <code>slice(0)</code>. If this were not present, the <code>sort</code> method would augment the original data directly (which is an unusual characteristic peculiar to <code>sort</code>). This would mean both the table <em>and</em> the mobile-width list structure would be rebuilt in the DOM. Since there are no sorting controls provided for the list structure, this is an unnecessary performance hit. </p> <h2 id="demo">Demo</h2> <p><a href="https://heydon.github.io/react-sortable-table-demo/">The complete demo</a>, including row headers, selective scrolling, the alternative representation for mobile, and the sorting functionality is available on Github.</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://github.com/Heydon/react-sortable-table-demo">Code on Github</a></li> <li><a href="https://heydon.github.io/react-sortable-table-demo/">Demo page</a></li> </ul> <h2 id="conclusion">Conclusion</h2> <p>Yes, <a href="http://adrianroselli.com/2017/11/hey-its-still-ok-to-use-tables.html">it's still okay to use tables</a>. Just don't use them if you don't need them and, when you <em>do</em> need them, structure them in a logical and expected way.</p> <h3 id="checklist">Checklist</h3> <ul> <li>Don't use tables just for layout or, to be more clear, <strong>don't use tables for anything but tabular data</strong>.</li> <li>Always include at least column headers <em>or</em> row headers.</li> <li>Sorting functionality is nice, but don't include it if it isn't needed. The 'Grindcore bands' example doesn't really need sorting because there's not much data in total. Allow switching it on or off with a <code>sortable</code> prop.</li> <li>Make sure the visual design of the table is clear, with obvious divisions between cells, and highlighted headers. To make it easier to scan rows, you may want to consider alternating row colors for a 'zebra' effect.</li> </ul> ]]>

<![CDATA[ <p>The key difference between a website and a web app is… highly contested. On the whole, I'd say the more links there are, the more site-like, and the more buttons, the more app-like. If it includes a page with a form, it's probably a kind of site. If it essentially <em>is</em> a form, you might call it an app. In any case, your web 'product' is really just interactive content, consumed and transmitted by an app we call a 'browser'.</p> <p>One thing that certainly makes a web page <em>feel</em> more like a desktop app is statefulness. Web pages that undergo changes as you are operating them are something quite unlike web pages that just load and unload as you click hyperlinks.</p> <p>Sometimes the user might instigate a change in state. Sometimes another user might affect the app remotely, in real time. Occasionally, the app might be subject to environmental and time-based events independent of user interaction. In each case, it's important users are kept abreast of changing state, which is a question of notifying them.</p> <p>In this article, I'll be looking at notification components and how they can increase confidence in the use of web applications, in an inclusive way.</p> <hr> <h2 id="drawingattention">Drawing attention</h2> <p>One of the biggest challenges in creating usable interfaces is knowing when to draw attention to something. Over-sharing may be considered a nuisance, but under-sharing might make the user feel they are missing critical information. This makes some hesitant, even where there is really nothing they "need to know" at the time.</p> <p>Then there's the <em>how</em>. Broadly speaking, there are two kinds of messages which need two different approaches to be accessible:</p> <ol> <li>Messages asking users to take action </li> <li><em>Just FYI</em> messages</li> </ol> <p>Typically, a message asking a user to do something would form the content of a dialog window (or inline disclosure), and be accompanied by a choice of action buttons. Because the keyboard operator will need to access those buttons, focus must be moved into the dialog.</p> <p>For the purpose of this article, what I mean by "notification" is a message that just lets you know what's going on. This may be so you can choose to take action later, or it may be to assure you of an event having taken place already.</p> <p>In screen reader and keyboard accessibility terms, it's important that focus is <em>not</em> moved to such messages. If there is nothing to be done with the tool, you don't put the tool in the person's hand. Despite this, moving focus has endured as a 'best practice'. Why? Because focusing an element has, traditionally, been the most reliable way to get that element and its contents announced in screen readers.</p> <figure> <img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/02/illustration1.svg" alt="Shows focus being moved to a notification, triggering announcement in the screen reader"> <figcaption>"Okay great. But where am I? What do I do now?"</figcaption> </figure> <p>Fortunately, we have live regions to help us break this habit.</p> <h2 id="liveregions101">Live regions 101</h2> <p>We've used live regions before on Inclusive Components, but I'm going to take the time to give you a broad overview here.</p> <p>A live region is just a container element that sets a perimeter around 'live' content: content that will be announced — by screen reader software — without user interaction, under certain conditions. By default, a live region will announce anything that is added or changed inside it.</p> <p>Somewhat perplexingly, there are two equivalent APIs for live regions: the <code>aria-live</code> attribute and live region ARIA roles. In most cases, you will want to use one of <code>role="status"</code> or <code>aria-live="polite"</code>. Using both simultaneously maximizes compatibility with different browser and assistive technology pairings:</p> <pre><code><div role="status" aria-live="polite"> </div> </code></pre> <p>Adding "Take a short break!" to this live region (as illustrated below) will trigger announcement immediately after the text node is inserted. It doesn't have to be a text node; it can be any markup.</p> <pre><code><div role="status" aria-live="polite"> Take a short break! </div> </code></pre> <p>Now the "Take a short break!" message's arrival in the interface can be seen and heard simultaneously, creating a parity between the visual and (screen reader assisted) aural experience. It is not the <em>same</em> experience, but it is a <a href="http://inclusivedesignprinciples.org/#provide-comparable-experience"><em>comparable</em> </a> one: it serves the same purpose.</p> <p>And everyone should take a periodic screen break.</p> <h3 id="invisibleliveregions">Invisible live regions</h3> <p>Sometimes, to create an overall comparable experience, a little extra aural information may be needed as a supplement. For example, when a user clicks an 'add to cart' button, the interface's response may be to animate the product moving into the cart. A direct translation of this may be a whooshing and clunking sound, but I suspect a visually hidden live region stating "product added successfully" (or similar) would be a lot clearer.</p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/02/illustration2.svg" alt="A packet of quinoa dog sweets is dragged onto the shopping cart symbol, triggering the readout of 'Quinoa dog sweets added to cart' as it is added"></p> <p>Adding a live region to a page already containing the content you wish to be announced is not reliable. There should be at least some time between the live region being appended to the DOM and the content being appended to the live region.</p> <p>For simply making screen readers "say things" alongside events in your scripts, I have <a href="https://github.com/Heydon/on-demand-live-region">created a small module</a>. Here's a hypothetical instantiation, using default settings:</p> <pre><code>const liveRegion = new OnDemandLiveRegion() liveRegion.say('Take a short break!') </code></pre> <p>Since the script creates hidden ARIA live regions and populates them on the fly, it makes communicating to screen readers procedurally trivial. However, in most cases — and in the case of status messages especially — we want to be communicating to <em>users</em>. Not users running screen readers or users <em>not</em> running screen readers; just users. Live regions make it easy to communicate through visual and aural channels simultaneously.</p> <h2 id="achatapplication">A chat application</h2> <p>In a chat application (something like Slack, say, where most everything happens in real time) there are a number of opportunities for status messages. For example:</p> <ul> <li>Users coming online</li> <li>Users being added to channels</li> <li>Users replying to your messages</li> <li>Users 'reacting' to your messages</li> </ul> <p>All of these types of messages coming in all the time is going to quickly become distracting and irritating, especially in their aural form. You can avert your eyes, but not your ears.</p> <p>We would need to do a couple of things to make the experience more tolerable:</p> <ul> <li>Restrict messages only to suitable contexts and situations</li> <li>Give the user control over messaging verbosity</li> </ul> <h3 id="restrictingmessagestocontexts">Restricting messages to contexts</h3> <p>Something I noticed recently while running a screen reader on one browser tab was that I could hear live regions rattling off updates from another open tab, not visible to me. The only solution was to close down the hidden tab. Not ideal, because I would have liked to switch back and forth between them.</p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/02/illustration3.svg" alt="Two browser tabs, with one in the foreground corresponding to the open page. The unselected tab has 'bla bla bla' being read out."></p> <p>For a sighted user, unseen is unknown. It doesn't matter if the messages keep getting displayed. But, for screen reader users (blind or otherwise), we need to silence output for hidden tabs. We can do this by querying <code>document.hidden</code> within the <code>visibilitychange</code> event from the <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Page_Visibility_API">Page Visibility API</a> and switching the live region between active and inactive. Inactive live regions take <code>role="none"</code> and/or <code>aria-live="off"</code>.</p> <p>Here's how that would work:</p> <pre><code>const notifications = document.getElementById('notifications'); document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => { let setting = document.hidden ? ['none', 'off'] : ['status', 'polite']; notification.setAttribute('role', setting[0]); notification.setAttribute('aria-live', setting[1]); }); </code></pre> <div role="complementary"> <h4>Your setup may vary</h4> <p>It's worth noting that some combinations of screen reader software and browser automatically silence at least some types of live region for hidden or unfocused tabs and windows. However, you can't rely on all your users having these setups and — where they don't — the experience is very off-putting.</p> </div> <h4 id="conversations">Conversations</h4> <p>Even when inside the open tab for the chat application, you won't want to be inundated by a flurry of any and all notifications. Visually, it could get irritating; aurally it almost <em>certainly</em> will. </p> <p>Knowing when to notify the user is a question of determining what activity they are currently engaged in. For example, users probably aren't interested in the messages of users not posting in the current thread, or the arrival online of users they have no history of engaging with in the past.</p> <p>On the other hand, if the user is focused on the text input for a thread and a new message pops in, they're probably going to want to know about it. In this case, the message would just appear if you're a sighted user. For a blind screen reader user, you make the new message its own notification with a live region.</p> <p>The <code>aria-relevant</code> attribute controls which kinds of changes to the live region are considered worthy of readout. In this case, only newly added messages are really of interest so we set <code>aria-relevant="additions"</code> on the parent element for the message stream.</p> <figure> <img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/02/illustration4.svg" alt="Messages appear above a text input labeled your message. The messages are in a container with aria-relevant equals additions applied to it. The input is focused."> <figcaption>When the new mesage, in grey, appears, only its contents — and not the contents of the other messages — are announced in screen readers.</figcaption> </figure> <p>Removed or edited messages would not be re-announced, but edited messages <em>should</em> remain discoverable. Hence, the markup for messages should be well-formed and semantically clear, using a list (<code><ul></code>) structure to group them together.</p> <pre><code><h1>Self care chat</h1> <div role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-relevant="additions"> <ul class="messages"> <li> <h2>Heydon, <small>22 minutes ago</small>:</h2> <p>Take a screen break. It's been 15 hours.</p> </li> <li> <h2>Heydon:</h2> <p>Oh, I guess you are already.</p> </li> </ul> <div> <form> <label for="message">Your message</label> <textarea id="message"></textarea> <button type="submit">Post</button> </form> </code></pre> <p>When that last item is appended to the master list, screen reader users hear "Heydon: Oh, I guess you are already." Arguably, you should append each message with the word 'message' to differentiate messages from other notifications. We'll come to those shortly.</p> <p>One refinement might be that, if the screen reader user is <em>not</em> focused on the text input they should only hear a new message being announced if it addresses them directly — using an "@", say. We're not depriving these users; we're just not interrupting them during a different task, unless it's a specific 'hey I need you'.</p> <h2 id="flashmessages">Flash messages</h2> <p>Flash messages — little colored strips of text that appear above the 'action' of the page — are often employed to keep users abreast of changing state. A single ARIA live region will suffice for these non-actionable notifications.</p> <p>I'll come to how these should be designed shortly, but first we need to make sure they can be switched off. The first thing I do when I install an app like Skype is switch off the notification sounds, and for good reason.</p> <h3 id="thesettingsscreen">The settings screen</h3> <p>Designing a page that houses application settings does not require a feat of engineering. It's just headings, subheadings, and form controls. But, through lack of care, you can botch the information architecture and terminology. </p> <p>"General" and "Content" don't really mean anything as category names, for example. And hiding what you subjectively consider 'advanced' settings behind a tiny, hard to locate link doesn't help either. </p> <p>Word everything descriptively, and structure everything logically. Use standard form controls such as checkboxes, radio buttons, and sliders. The settings screen <a href="http://inclusivedesignprinciples.org/#give-control">gives users control</a> over how they use the application; don't make it an afterthought.</p> <div role="complementary"> <h4>Headings inside legends</h4> <p>When structuring (long) forms, it often helps to group related controls together inside <code><fieldset></code> elements. Then <code><legend></code> elements can be employed to provide 'group labels'. These are announced when screen reader users enter the fieldset and focus the first control. They give contextual information.</p> <p><code><legend></code>s tend to supplant headings, because otherwise you'd be labeling sections of the form twice. The trouble is, headings have their own advantages for screen reader navigation.</p> <p>Fortunately, <a href="http://w3c.github.io/html/sec-forms.html#the-legend-element">a recent change to the HTML spec</a> now allows you to author pages with headings inside your <code><legend></code>s: the best of both worlds. Here's the sort of structure, we should be going for:</p> <img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/02/illustration5_small.svg" alt="An h1 of settings followed by two sections: Change your password and Notifications, each introduced by h2 headings inside legends and grouped by fieldset containers."> </div> <p>Note that turning off a notification type would mean it no longer occurs visually or aurally (in screen reader output). It's likely that certain notifications would be much less desirable to many screen reader users, and they're more likely to turn them off. But everyone has the <em>same</em> control and can make decisions for themselves. We're not making assumptions for them.</p> <h3 id="differentiatingmessagetypes">Differentiating message types</h3> <p>Our singular live region may play host to a variety of notification types. Basic information will probably be most common, but there may be warnings, errors, and messages of congratulation — perhaps the user can earn awards for being a helpful member of the community.</p> <p>The general rule is that <strong>any part of an interface differentiated only by style and not content will be inaccessible</strong>. Things like shape, color, position are just not enough on their own to define something inclusively. In this case, the MVP for differentiating messages is therefore to preface with terms like "Error:", "Info:", "Congratulations:" or whatever is suitable. A bold style is typical.</p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/02/illustration10.svg" alt="Three different message types. A message starting 'congratulations' in green, a message starting 'error' in red and a message starting 'info' in blue."></p> <p>Should you wish to supplant the text with icons you'll have to be careful they are visually comprehensible, include alternative text for screen reader users, and are still visible where Windows High Contrast Mode is running.</p> <p>Try an optimized, inline SVG with a <code>fill</code> set to <code>currentColor</code> to honor high contrast mode. For alternative text, <code>aria-label</code> is not recommended because it is not picked up by translation services like Google's. The same, unfortunately, applies to any text (<code><title></code> or <code><text></code>, say) <em>inside</em> SVGs. The best we can do is insert some <a href="https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/fundamentals/hiding/#content-that-should-only-be-hidden-visually">visually hidden</a> text just for assistive software. It's ugly markup, but it works.</p> <pre><code><div role="status" aria-live="polite"> <div class="message award"> <p> <strong> <svg viewBox="0 0 20 20" focusable="false"> <use xlink:href="#star"></use> </svg> <span class="visually-hidden">Congratulations!</span> </strong> You've been awarded 6 fake internet points </p> </div> </div> </code></pre> <figure> <img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/02/illustration8.svg" alt="An empty dotted outline indicates the invisible span that reads " congratulations""=""> <figcaption>The hidden span would of course be completely invisible. The outline is shown here just to indicate its whereabouts.</figcaption> </figure> <h3 id="dismissingnotifications">Dismissing notifications</h3> <p>Working as a design consultant, I often see notification messages include little "✖️" buttons to dismiss them. </p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/02/illustration9.svg" alt="Notification with a cross symbol/button to its right hand side."></p> <p>While I always want to applaud efforts to put users in control of the interface, I'm not so sure in this case. I just don't think the ability to manually dismiss notifications is important enough to <em>bother</em> users with; it's not something worth encountering or having to think about. (There's also the issue of managing focus when the close button is removed from the DOM after being pressed, as covered in <a href="https://inclusive-components.design/a-todo-list/">A Todo List</a>).</p> <p>Instead, it's better the messages just disappear by themselves — after an appropriate amount of time. Here's a small script that lets you create notifications regions by type ('error', 'award', or 'info', say) and inject/remove notification messages after a chosen amount of time.</p> <pre><code>function Notifier(type, regionEl, duration) { this.regionEl = regionEl; this.duration = duration || 10000; this.type = type || 'info'; } Notifier.prototype.notify = function(message) { let note = document.createElement('p'); note.innerHTML = ` <svg viewBox="0 0 20 20" focusable="false"> <use xlink:href="#${this.type}"></use> </svg> <span class="visually-hidden">${this.type}:</span> ${message} `; this.regionEl.appendChild(note); window.setTimeout(() => { this.regionEl.removeChild(note) }, this.duration); } const infoNotifications = new Notifier( 'info', document.getElementById('notifications'), 5000 ); infoNotifications.notify('Heydon666 has joined this group.'); </code></pre> <p>(<strong>Note:</strong> The 'type' string is used both for the inline SVG reference and as the alternative text for the icon.)</p> <p>But what if the user misses notifications come and go? Not a problem. Notifications should only refer to things that are discoverable elsewhere in the updated interface.</p> <p>A couple of examples: If the notification refers to <strong>@Heydon666</strong> coming online, you'll be able to discover they're around because they have appeared in the list of active users, or have their status updated. For the 'awards' example, the interface should keep track in the user's profile page. A chronology of awards is typical.</p> <p><img src="https://inclusive-components.design/content/images/2018/02/illustration7_small.svg" alt="List of awards by date."></p> <h2 id="conclusion">Conclusion</h2> <p>Thanks to the marvelous "you add it, I say it" nature of ARIA live regions, the technical implementation of inclusive notification could hardly be simpler. That leaves you to perfect the clarity of form and language.</p> <p>The biggest and most important task actually has nothing to do with the notification component itself. It's all in the structure and presentation of the permanent history into which each notification message only offers a fleeting glimpse. As ever, structuring content is paramount, even where it pertains to dynamic events inside realtime web applications.</p> <h3 id="checklist">Checklist</h3> <ul> <li>Don't use <a href="http://juicystudio.com/article/wai-aria_live-regions_updated.php"><code>aria-atomic="true"</code></a> unless you want all the contents of a live region announced whenever there's any change within it.</li> <li>Be judicious in your use of visually hidden live regions. Most content should be seen <em>and</em> heard.</li> <li>Distinguish parts of your interface in content or with content and style, but never just with style.</li> <li>Do not announce everything that changes on the page. A very popular carousel plugin that shall remain nameless announces the arrival of each slide as it comes into view. A huge irritant, and only comparable to a sighted user's experience if the carousel is set to track their eye movements and always remain at the center of their gaze.</li> <li>Be <em>very</em> wary of <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/notification">Desktop notifications</a> for your site. I have never come across a site for which I wanted these needy and obstructive messages to be permitted.</li> </ul> ]]>
